item.title: Adaptive Human-AI Collaboration: Taxonomies and the MCAL Reference Model
item.description:
Adaptive Human-AI Collaboration: Taxonomies and the MCAL Reference Model

Artificial intelligence is shifting from a static decision-support tool to an adaptive collaborator that must sense context, decide when and how to intervene, and improve through repeated interaction with humans individually and in groups.

🔍 Overview

This paper reports a review of adaptive human‑AI collaboration literature through a closed‑loop lens.

📚 Review Methodology

  • Iterative identification
  • Staged selection against explicit criteria
  • Structured extraction
  • Taxonomy‑driven synthesis
  • Snowballing

The authors analyzed 50 reviewed works using this process.

🧩 Taxonomies

The review contributes three taxonomies:

  1. Multimodal Context Modeling – spans from individual states to collective states such as group engagement and participation equality.
  2. Uncertainty‑Aware Intervention – covers uncertainty sources, estimation and calibration mechanisms, an intervention repertoire that ranges from explanation modulation and deferral to group facilitation, and intervention policies.
  3. Longitudinal Co‑Adaptation and Synergy‑Oriented Evaluation.

⚙️ MCAL Reference Model

The three taxonomies are integrated into MCAL, a dual‑timescale Multimodal Co‑Adaptation Loop reference model. MCAL is instantiated on a mixed human‑robot workspace, and the authors walk every stage of the loop through one concrete setting to show what each taxonomy cell holds in practice.

📅 Publication Details

  • Title of host publication: Companion of the INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON MULTIMODAL INTERACTION (ICMI Companion ‘26)
  • Publisher: Association for Computing Machinery
  • Publication date: 5 Oct 2026 (Published – 5 Oct 2026)
  • Event: 28th ACM International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI 2026), Napoli, Italy, 5‑9 Oct 2026
  • Keywords: human‑AI collaboration, literature review, multimodal sensing, collective states, Uncertainty, Trust Calibration, feedback loops

💡 Why it matters

Meta‑analytic evidence shows that human‑AI combinations often fail to outperform the best of either partner alone, and the enabling literature remains fragmented across multimodal sensing, uncertainty quantification, reliance and delegation, facilitation, and teaming. By organizing this fragmented work into unified taxonomies and a closed‑loop reference model, the paper provides a structured foundation for building adaptive human‑AI collaborators that can sense context, handle uncertainty, and co‑adapt over time.

Source: Adaptive Human-AI Collaboration: A Review of Multimodal Context Modeling, Uncertainty-Aware Intervention, and Longitudinal Co-Adaptation

item.title: Study Maps How Mixed Human‑AI Groups Form Consensus
item.description:
Study Maps How Mixed Human‑AI Groups Form Consensus

A recent experiment examined how mixing large language model (LLM) agents with humans in a collaborative description game changes the way groups reach consensus.

🔍 Overview

  • LLM agents are moving from being simple tools to active participants in human groups.
  • The research asked how this growing presence reshapes consensus formation.
  • Participants played a description game where shared conventions emerged through repeated rounds of random pairwise communication.

🧩 How it works

  • Human participants and LLM agents were combined in varying proportions.
  • Each round involved a random pair communicating to describe a target, allowing conventions to develop over time.
  • Agent influence stems from a shared linguistic prior that places agents near one another in expression space and from relatively stable expression choices across rounds.
  • Humans initially resist adopting expressions from partners perceived as AI but gradually yield to conformity pressure.

⚙️ Key findings

  • Three distinct regimes of consensus formation emerged as the proportion of LLM agents changed:
    • Low agent proportions → human‑led consensus.
    • Intermediate proportions → disruption of convergence.
    • High proportions → strong consensus that shifts toward agent‑led conventions.
  • The regimes differ not only in convergence strength but also in semantic grounding and communicative form:
    • Human‑led consensus is more concrete, holistic, and grounded in shared real‑world analogies.
    • Agent‑led consensus is more abstract, less information‑dense, and more geometrically segmented.
Regime Agent proportion Consensus type Characteristics
Low Low Human‑led Concrete, holistic, grounded in real‑world analogies
Intermediate Intermediate Disrupted convergence —
High High Agent‑led Abstract, less information‑dense, geometrically segmented

💡 Why it matters

  • The study provides evidence that AI composition can shape the emergence, content, and perceived legitimacy of group norms.
  • Agent proportion and transparency emerge as important design variables for human‑AI systems.
  • Understanding these dynamics helps designers anticipate how mixed groups will develop shared language and norms.

#humanAI #consensus #LLMagents #collectivebehavior

Source: AI agents reshape consensus formation in human groups
